His expression settled into something that wasn't quite a smile — too waterlogged for that, too recently acquainted with the bottom of a hallway — but still showed the smallest spark of his usual dramatic flair. "...You do know those walls are breakable, right?" Ch 9 – Threshold The school had stopped pretending to have a floor. Not entirely — the taller ones could still find it if they stretched, toes scraping tile in the brief spaces between surges, just enough contact to push off from before the next wave took it away again. For the rest, it was just swimming, burning through limited reserves as they tried not to think about how close the ceiling was getting. Nobody said it out loud. There was a direction now, which was better than the alternative. Better than standing in the foyer, waiting for the moment the building made the decision for them. They had a direction and they moved in it and that was enough to keep the other thought at arm's length. The building had other opinions about all of this, naturally. The flashlight barely reached. Orela kept it forward and kept moving, but the beam gave them maybe three feet of visibility before the chaos swallowed it — water and noise and darkness pressing in from every direction. The school doing what it had been doing all night but with far less patience. The pipes were still screaming somewhere above them, muffled by the water but present, a constant high-pressure shriek that had stopped being startling a while ago and had become just another feature of the environment. Lockers banged open and shut along the walls in a violent rhythm. Ceiling tiles dropped without warning, each one landing with a slap of displaced water that soaked whoever was nearest, the spray cold and sharp against faces. It was a gauntlet, not a hallway. A hydraulic cage fight, and the school was winning. Conversation was functionally over. If you weren't close enough to shout directly into someone's ear, the water took your words before they arrived. Dwight kept his focus on his own breathing. In. Out. Arms moving. Head up. That was the whole job right now — not the ceiling, not the dark, not whatever was brushing past his legs in the churn. Just the breathing and the moving and the narrow column of air between his face and the surface. Anything to smother the panic skittering just under his skin. He wasn’t a good swimmer. Never had been. The graceless thrashing of it was eating his energy and burning out his muscles faster than he could recover. But he couldn’t stop. Couldn’t sink. He had to keep his mouth above the water. Something hit him broadside. A chunk of debris — metal, fast, heavy, the edge of a locker door catching him across the shoulder and spinning him sideways before he'd registered it coming. He went under. The dark closed over his head and the noise inverted, muffled and enormous simultaneously, and for one disorienting second there was no up. A hand caught him, painfully tight around his arm. He was yanked upward again, sputtering, hacking, blinking hard against the burn — only to find Danny clinging to him, wide-eyed and breathless, holding him up against the current. One hand was still locked around his arm, the other braced against the wall, his expression doing something complicated that resolved itself quickly into nothing at all. “Don’t drown on me, pencil neck,” Danny hissed, tight against his ear as he pulled him back to the wall edge. “I don’t want your death pinned on me unless it’s actually my doing.” It was clearly meant to sound threatening, but it ended up being somewhat of a comfort to Dwight. Even the killer couldn’t just let someone go out like that, it seemed. Orela twisted in the water again, light flashing over both of them. She was checking. Constantly. Refusing to let any of them vanish into the dark behind her. Her face was tight with effort. Eyes flicking between each survivor in turn — counting, clocking, making sure nobody had vanished into the dark between one glance and the next. The building had already demonstrated its opinion on unattended survivors and she wasn't giving it another opportunity. Danny was moving better than she'd expected, the water doing the work his legs couldn't fully manage on their own, the buoyancy buying him a temporary reprieve from the pressure of gravity against his own injuries. She noted the wheeze in his breathing, barely heard over the water, and filed it alongside the wet coughs that had started cropping up in the others. There was nothing she could really do about any of it from here, anyways. Leon had taken up a position at the edge of the group, shoulder-first into the current, methodically redirecting the debris that kept drifting in from the side passages. A cabinet corner. A floating shelf unit. Something that had been a door once and was now just waterlogged wood with ambitions. He caught them before they could find someone's head and shoved them aside without comment, jaw set, eyes forward. The building pushed back. The currents shifted without warning, tugging at legs from new angles, trying to bleed momentum out of the group and separate them one redirected stroke at a time. Ceiling tiles dropped in irregular intervals — not enough to be predictable, not random enough to be accidental — each one landing close enough to make a point. Debris drifted in from the hallway mouths like it had somewhere to be, and that somewhere was always directly in their path.
